newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Russia PM wants Norilsk probe,sale seen safe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Russia PM wants Norilsk probe,sale seen safe.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin called for an investigation on Wednesday into the sale of a controlling stake in Norilsk Nickel, as the row over a major controversial privatisation refused to go away.
"Questions over whether the tender was in accordance with current legislation will be looked at, irrespective of the results," he was quoted by Prime-Tass news agency as saying.
But a senior government source said an investigation into the legality of the auction run by its winner was unlikely to turn up sufficient grounds to reverse the deal.

The tender of the stake in one of the world's largest base and precious metals producers balanced on a knife edge until its conclusion on Tuesday. Chernomyrdin and other senior government officials had called for it to be suspended.
The source said they made a last-minute decision to allow the auction to go ahead, but only after Chernomyrdin said he viewed $250 million as a fair price for the stake.
ZAO Svift, a firm representing powerful Uneximbank, won the tender with a bid of $250 million. Uneximbank president Vladimir Potanin met Chernomyrdin on the morning of the sale.

The row over who gets what in the most aggressive phase yet of Russia's privatisation programme has not gone away just because the government at least temporarily dropped official objections to the Norilsk sale.
Rivals to Uneximbank may also challenge the sale.

"It is still too early to speak of a final victory for Uneximbank: competitors are already preparing a suit, demanding the results of yesterday's auction be cancelled," the business newspaper Kommersant Daily said on its front page on Wednesday.

Nezavisimaya Gazeta, owned by a financial group which competes with Uneximbank, said the auction could unleash a bitter war between rival banking groups that have emerged during the volatile post-Soviet economic transition in Russia.
"The victory of Uneximbank in the auction will launch a new, possibly the fiercest and therefore the final battle between rival banking groups," the paper said.

An elite group of businessmen and bankers united to help re-elect President Boris Yeltsin last year. They have also won some of the best spoils of privatisation recently, acquiring stakes in oil, and now telecoms and mining companies.
Uneximbank's Norilsk victory and July's win of a major stake in the Svyazinvest telecom firm, the biggest single Russian privatisation deal so far, have turned rivals green with envy.

While observers hailed Svyazinvest as Russia's fairest sale yet, Norilsk was widely viewed as less open, and the last hangover from the controversial shares-for-loans transfers of Russia's early phase of privatisation.
Uneximbank won management control of the 38 percent Norilsk stake, or 51 percent of voting shares, in return for lending the government $170 million in 1995.
Conflicts of interest in the Norilsk auction have raised more than a few eyebrows.
Uneximbank deputy chairman Dmitry Ushakov held the deciding vote in the tender committee, split between state and Uneximbank supporters.
And MFK Moscow Partners, linked to Uneximbank's Bank MFK (IFCI in English), actually organised the tender.
"The organisers of the competition are also taking part," Yevgeny Yasin, minister without portfolio, was quoted in Wednesday's Izvestiya newspaper as saying.
"The clear impression is that everything was done intentionally so that the shares were sold at a low price and to a buyer who was known in advance."
